note: One entry per integrated exploit family. Everything here is derived from a pinned primary source; grades: B = byte/instruction proven, A = necessarily derived, K = source self-report (unverified), H = hypothesis, X = checked and refuted, BLOCKED = not provable with named unblocking condition.

families.name: PPPwn -- PPPoE/sppp LCP-Configure-Request heap overflow

root_cause.summary: The kernel's PPP implementation copies the option payload of an inbound LCP/IPCP Configure-Request into a fixed-size buffer without validating the length taken from the packet, so a peer-controlled length overflows a heap object of the pppoe softc.
root_cause.why_grade: the upstream writeup is the HackerOne report (CVE-2006-4304, H1 #2177925) which is not public; the reconstruction rests on the exploit's own packet construction and on the fact that the overflow payload is built as an mbuf/LLE-shaped object (build_overflow_lle in pppwn.py)
evidence: pppwn.py:184 lcp_negotiation() and :213 ipcp_negotiation() drive the Configure-Request exchange that the overflow rides in
pppwn.py:360 build_overflow_lle() constructs the object that must land in the overflowed slot: pppoe_softc-relative pointers, an rwlock, lle_head/lle_free chain fields
stage1/offsets.h resolves pppoe_softc_list, nd6_llinfo_timer, cc_cpu, callwheelsize, kernel_map, kmem_alloc, kproc_create per firmware -- the primitive set the family needs

lifecycle.claim: the overflow corrupts a heap object adjacent to the softc; the exploit then frees and reallocates to place a controlled LLE
inbound Configure-Request options are parsed into a fixed buffer; the length is peer-controlled

trigger.who: unauthenticated peer on the same L2 segment (PPPoE discovery + session)
trigger.precondition: kernel PPP/PPPoE support reachable from the network stack; no userland privilege needed
evidence: the whole exploit runs from a host on the segment with no console access

privilege_boundary.requires: L2 adjacency; PPPoE discovery to get a session id
privilege_boundary.note: the only family in this set whose entry is not a syscall at all -- reachability cannot be read off sysent

primitives_required: heap overflow with controlled length and content
deterministic reclaim of the freed object (socket/LLE spray)
kernel ROP or a kexec-style syscall hijack to leave ring 3

firmware.vulnerable: 7.00 - 11.00 (all firmwares the exploit ships offsets for)
firmware.fixed: after 11.00 (the vendor fix is not public; the exploit has no 13.52 offsets)

families.label_reasoning: 9.00 is in the exploit's own supported list (POSITIVE = the vulnerable code shape is present). 13.52 is outside it and the exploit ships no offsets for it (NEGATIVE = no evidence the shape survived; this is an assumption of the source, not a proof).
families.falsification: show a 13.52 image in which the LCP/IPCP Configure-Request option copy still uses a peer-controlled length without a bound check

families.name: Lapse -- aio_multi_delete unlocked entry-array race

root_cause.summary: In _aio_multi_delete() the branch that handles a submission with more than one remaining id decrements obj->ao_rem_ids and frees obj->ao_entries[req_idx] without taking the write lock; the slot is only NULLed afterwards, so a second thread can read the same slot and free the entry twice.
root_cause.why_grade: the vulnerable C body is quoted verbatim in lapse.mjs (comment above race_one(), reproduced from the author's disassembly) and every field it names is a real structure access
evidence: lapse.mjs:493-537 -- the quoted _aio_multi_delete/free_queue_entry body with the inline marker 'BUG: wlock not acquired on this path'
lapse.mjs:538 race_one() -- two threads pinned to one core, a pthread barrier, then aio_multi_delete on the same id range; thr_suspend_ucontext is used to stretch the window inside soclose()
lapse.mjs:1510 -- sysent[661] is taken over for the kexec primitive (offset 0x1107f00 on 9.00)
module/chain.mjs:85-89 -- syscall numbers: aio_multi_delete=662, aio_multi_wait=663, aio_multi_poll=664, aio_multi_cancel=666, aio_submit_cmd=669

lifecycle.claim: id_rlock() read-locks the id table; the >1 branch then mutates ao_rem_ids and the entry array while holding only that read view
free_queue_entry() drops the file reference (fdrop) and frees the entry with M_AIO_REQS2
the file reference survives long enough to reach soclose(), which is where the exploit stretches the window

trigger.who: any process that can call aio_multi_delete (662) on a multi-entry submission
trigger.precondition: an SceAIO parameter with more than one submitted id; two threads on the same core for deterministic interleaving

privilege_boundary.requires: a valid aio context and a multi-id submission -- no root, no device node
privilege_boundary.note: the exploit uses cpuset_setaffinity + rtprio_thread + pthread barriers to make the race deterministic; those are all unprivileged

primitives_required: controlled double free of an aio_entry (128-byte class)
reclaim with an aliased object (the exploit uses IPv6 routing-header sprays)
a kernel call primitive (sysent[661] hijack to a jmp [rsi] gadget)
families.label_reasoning: 9.00 is inside the source's own supported range and our image resolves the very sysent[661] slot the exploit writes (0x1107f00). 13.52 is outside the range, so the fix is expected; the label is an expectation from the source, not a measurement.
families.falsification: show that on 13.52 the >1 branch of aio_multi_delete still mutates ao_rem_ids and frees the entry array slot while holding only the read lock
counter_evidence: our 13.52 image is not pristine (kpatched), so an unchanged-looking function could be a patch artefact rather than the shipped code

families.name: Relapse / exFAThax v2 -- exFAT driver UAF class

root_cause.summary: exFAT driver use-after-free of a driver object, reachable by mounting a crafted image; the family is the pOOBs4 class re-instantiated for 13.02-13.52 and fixed in 14.00.
root_cause.why_grade: the research repo states the class and the FW range but publishes no root-cause body; the primary report (H1) is not public. Our own R3 round did validate a POS/NEG pair by running the published code in an emulation harness, which is recorded as internal evidence, not as a primary source.
evidence: ps4-13xx-research/README.md -- 'exFAThax v2: kernel panic confirmed on FW 13.04', 'Relapse 13.02-13.52', 'fixed 14.00'
the same README lists the 14.00 candidates the authors consider unpatched (semctl/semop/tty TIOCSCTTY), which is the family's own follow-up surface

lifecycle.claim: a crafted image drives an object through mount -> directory parse -> free while a second reference survives

trigger.who: any process that can mount or open a crafted exFAT image (USB media path is the classic one)
trigger.precondition: a filesystem view the kernel parses on attach; no privilege beyond the media path

privilege_boundary.requires: media attach (USB) or an image mount the sandbox permits
privilege_boundary.note: the reachability is physical-media shaped, which is why the family is not a remote primitive

primitives_required: UAF with a controllable free point
reclaim of the freed object with attacker-influenced content
a write-what-where or call primitive out of the reclaimed object
families.label_reasoning: 13.52 is inside the family's range (POSITIVE). 9.00 carries the *earlier* instance of the same class (pOOBs4, fixed 9.03), so a 9.00 image cannot serve as a negative for this instance; it is marked NOT_APPLICABLE instead of being forced into a label.
families.falsification: show that on 13.52 no exFAT parse path frees a driver object while another reference to it stays live
counter_evidence: no public root-cause body exists for this family; any code-level claim needs our own emulation evidence, which is not part of Sprint 1

families.name: Afterglow -- kqueue knote/clone UAF on the fd teardown path

root_cause.summary: A kqueue note array outlives the object it points at: notes hang on descriptors that were cloned and freed earlier, so knote_fdclose()/kqueue_close() walk dead memory; the exploit stretches the window with a device open/close and hijacks a close entry.
root_cause.why_grade: the kernel stage's own writeup ('the same as in the Lua version') is not in this repo; the reconstruction below is read off the code, and the family is therefore deliberately used as a BLIND test -- its labels are held out from the scanner.
evidence: afterglow.js around the 'one attempt at the bug' comment -- a unit is spent only when its clone is freed; the free is the window
afterglow.js 'exit1() also runs knote_fdclose() for every descriptor, and that does not go through fo_close' -- the teardown path the exploit relies on
afterglow.js 'kqueue_close takes the note array length from ...' -- length read from the structure itself
TECHNICAL.md -- 25 kernel text sites covered by the PATCHES table plus 10 written by the bootstrap stub

lifecycle.claim: notes survive the free of the descriptor copies they were registered on
closing a clone frees the note-owning object while a foreign queue still references it
open/close of the device node is the spray and the close path is the hijack target

trigger.who: a process that can call kqueue/kevent/open/close/ioctl (all unprivileged)
trigger.precondition: one free unit per boot; a warm second attempt is not equivalent (the handles are not defused on failure)

privilege_boundary.entry: syscalls 362 (kqueue) / 363 (kevent) plus the device-node close path
privilege_boundary.requires: nothing beyond the browser host's syscall primitive
privilege_boundary.note: the exploit's own host boundary is only {syscall, buffer address, typed read/write, keepAlive}

primitives_required: deterministic reclaim of a freed note-array owner
controlled fo_close entry (the exploit points each copy's close entry at a stub)
families.label_reasoning: Blind test: the scanner must reach this subsystem without being told. Labels are held out of every rule and every assertion that the scanner uses.
families.falsification: show that on 13.52 every knote registered on a cloned fd is destroyed before the clone's owner is freed, and that kqueue_close() never trusts a length read from the structure
counter_evidence: the exploit ships one free unit per boot and fails silently if another allocation wins the hole -- a shape that is easy to over-claim from static code
